walkthrough:
**What controls volatility?**

Volatility is how easily a liquid turns to vapour. To evaporate, molecules must overcome the attractions between molecules.

Stronger intermolecular forces mean less volatility:

**Identify the forces in halogens**

Both chlorine, $Cl_2$, and iodine, $I_2$, are simple non-polar diatomic molecules. They have no permanent dipole, so they cannot have permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.

The only force between them is temporary dipole-induced dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces.

**Compare $Cl_2$ and $I_2$**

London forces depend on how polarisable the electron cloud is. Iodine is much larger with many more electrons (53 per atom versus 17 for chlorine).

$$ \text{more electrons} \rightarrow \text{more polarisable} \rightarrow \text{stronger London forces} $$

**Link to observation**

Stronger London forces in $I_2$ need more energy to break, so iodine is a solid at room temperature while chlorine is a gas. That is why iodine is less volatile.

options.A: Electronegativity affects polarity within a bond, not repulsion between non-polar molecules. Both $Cl_2$ molecules are neutral and non-polar, so there is no extra repulsion idea. This confuses an atomic property with intermolecular forces.
options.B: Correct. $I_2$ has far more electrons than $Cl_2$, so its electron cloud is larger and more polarisable. This creates larger temporary dipoles and stronger London dispersion forces, which require more energy to overcome, making iodine less volatile.
options.C: It is true that the I-I bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond, but bond energy is about the covalent bond inside the molecule. Volatility depends on breaking forces between molecules, not breaking the molecule itself, so this is irrelevant.
options.D: Both $Cl_2$ and $I_2$ are non-polar because the two atoms are identical and share electrons equally. They have zero permanent dipole, so permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces do not exist here. This is a common trap.
